newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures claw back from Thursday's dive.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures claw back from Thursday's dive.

text.p: Bunds spent much of Friday clawing back some of Thursday's 1.5 point loss in what traders said was largely thin trade ahead of the weekend.

Dealers who had returned to their desks following the Christmas holiday were reluctant to push Bunds too high ahead of what could be an important week next week with both German gross domestic product and unemployment data due.
At 1534 GMT, the DTB Bund futures contract was up 29 basis points at 99.69, not far from the day's high of 99.74.
"It has been a fairly strong day," one trader said. "But it is hard to be bullish just yet."
German debt was little moved by a pair of German economic indicators -- trade and industrial production.
The production figures, which showed a 1.6 percent month-on-month gain, were stronger than expected, but failed to worry bond traders much.
"It is only one of 12 numbers," said Michael Hochguertel, market economist at BHF-Bank. "It was not strong enough to bring a really heavy impact."
The trade figures showed the German economy continuing to benefit from exports, but failed as usual to excite much interest among Bund investors.

Bund futures took much of their strength on the day from Treasuries. The Bund/T-note spread stood at 65 basis points late in the afternoon, down from a 68 basis point spread at the same time on Thursday.

Traders said they expect to seen Bunds trading between 99.28 and 99.90 before the unemployment and GDP data. Analysts said the bottom end of that range is an important level for Bunds. Brian Clapp, analyst at Stone & McCarthy, described the level as a "corrective bottom" from December 13. A breach of the point could establish a period of lower highs, he said.
Traders said they see demand remaining strong for the short-end of the German yield curve, one of the main factors behind a sharp steepening of the two- to 10-year curve on Thursday.
Worries about the long-end of the curve, meanwhile, are being fanned by an increase in supply coming from a new 10-year issue, details of which will be announced next week.
The German government in late December released plans for first quarter debt issuance of as much as 54 billion marks, including a 10-year Bund totaling as much as 15 billion.
